title: A Call Across the Bus: Requests, Responses, Timeouts and the Command That Ran Twice

questions.question: A call gets no answer. What can the caller conclude?
options: That the request never reached the server, so it is safe to assume nothing was done
Nothing: the request may not have arrived, or may have been done with the answer lost, or the answer may be late
That the server is dead, since a live server always answers
That the work was done and only the answer was lost, so the call can be treated as complete
questions.explanation: Lost on the way there, done with the answer lost, or merely late: the three look the same from the caller's side. A timeout is not knowing.

questions.question: Why does each call carry a number?
options: So the server can do the calls in the order they were made
So the client can count how many calls it has made in total
So a lost call can be detected by a gap in the numbers
So an answer is matched to the call it answers: two calls answered in the other order each got their own answer
questions.explanation: With two calls in flight, the next answer to arrive need not be for the older one. The number is what ties each answer to its own call.

questions.question: A call timed out and its answer arrives. What happens?
options: The call completes after all, since the answer is the truth
The answer is unwanted: counted and discarded, and the call stays timed out
The call is sent again, so that the answer can be matched to a fresh attempt
The server is asked to undo the work
questions.explanation: The caller has already acted on the timeout. Letting a late answer change the call's state would give it a result it has already treated as a failure.

questions.question: With no retries, 155 of 300 calls timed out. How many times did the work run?
options: 214: for 69 calls the work was done and the client was told it had failed
145, once for each call that completed
155, once for each call that timed out
300, once for each call made
questions.explanation: A request that arrives is carried out even if its answer is then lost. So the work ran more often than the client was told it had.

questions.question: What keeps a retried call from doing the work twice?
options: A longer timeout, so that fewer calls are retried: 300 runs for 300 calls
A limit of one retry for each call: 300 runs for 300 calls, against 446 with six retries
A server that remembers the answers it gave by (client, number) and returns the remembered one for a repeat: 300 runs for 300 calls, against 446 for a server that forgot
Sending each retry with a new number: 300 runs for 300 calls, against 446 with the same number
questions.explanation: A retry is the same request again. If the server keeps the answer under the client and the number, a repeat gets the old answer and the work is not done twice.

questions.question: Why is a repeated gripper command harmless and a repeated dispense command not?
options: The gripper closing twice leaves it closed, and dispensing twice gives two
The gripper's server remembers its answers and the dispenser's does not
Closing takes longer than dispensing, so the repeat arrives too late to matter
A dispense command is sent best effort and a gripper command reliable
questions.explanation: The first is idempotent and the second is not, so the second needs the server to remember. Closing a closed gripper changes nothing. Dispensing again gives a second dose, so that service must not be run twice for one request.
